1.1.iast: dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre samavetā yuyutsavaḥ . | māmakāḥ pāṇḍavāścaiva kimakurvata sañjaya
1.1.gloss: Dhritarashtra: On the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, gathered and eager to fight — what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do, Sanjaya?
1.1.note: The opening word-pair 'dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre' is itself read two ways: a literal place name, and a pun — 'the field where dharma is at stake'.

1.21.gloss: Arjuna to Krishna: Position my chariot between the two armies, unfailing one.

1.22.iast: yāvadetānnirīkṣe'haṃ yoddhukāmānavasthitān . | kairmayā saha yoddhavyamasmin raṇasamudyame
1.22.gloss: So that I may see those who stand here drawn up, longing for the fight, and know whom I am to face in this undertaking.

1.28.iast: kṛpayā parayāviṣṭo viṣīdannidamabravīt . | dṛṣṭvemaṃ svajanaṃ kṛṣṇa yuyutsuṃ samupasthitam
1.28.gloss: Sanjaya: Overwhelmed by great compassion, grieving, he said — Arjuna: seeing these my own people assembled, Krishna, eager for battle...

1.29.iast: sīdanti mama gātrāṇi mukhaṃ ca pariśuṣyati . | vepathuśca śarīre me romaharṣaśca jāyate
1.29.gloss: My limbs sink, my mouth goes dry, my body trembles, my hair stands on end.

1.30.iast: gāṇḍīvaṃ sraṃsate hastāttvakcaiva paridahyate . | na ca śaknomyavasthātuṃ bhramatīva ca me manaḥ
1.30.gloss: The Gandiva bow slips from my hand, my skin burns; I cannot stand steady, and my mind whirls.

1.41.iast: adharmābhibhavātkṛṣṇa praduṣyanti kulastriyaḥ . | strīṣu duṣṭāsu vārṣṇeya jāyate varṇasaṅkaraḥ
1.41.gloss: When lawlessness overwhelms, Krishna, the women of the family are corrupted; and when women are corrupted, Varshneya, mixing of varnas is born.
1.41.note: Arjuna's own argument, not Krishna's. The social-anxiety logic here (women → lineage purity → varna order) is exactly what later critics such as Ambedkar targeted.

1.42.iast: saṅkaro narakāyaiva kulaghnānāṃ kulasya ca . | patanti pitaro hyeṣāṃ luptapiṇḍodakakriyāḥ
1.42.gloss: That mixing drags down the destroyers of the family and the family itself; their ancestors fall, cut off from the rice-ball and water offerings.

1.47.iast: evamuktvārjunaḥ saṅkhye rathopastha upāviśat . | visṛjya saśaraṃ cāpaṃ śokasaṃvignamānasaḥ
1.47.gloss: Having spoken thus, Arjuna sat down on the chariot seat, casting aside bow and arrows, his mind drowned in sorrow.

2.11.iast: aśocyānanvaśocastvaṃ prajñāvādāṃśca bhāṣase . | gatāsūnagatāsūṃśca nānuśocanti paṇḍitāḥ
2.11.gloss: Krishna: You grieve for what deserves no grief, and speak what sounds like wisdom; the truly learned grieve neither for the living nor for the dead.

2.13.iast: dehino'sminyathā dehe kaumāraṃ yauvanaṃ jarā . | tathā dehāntaraprāptirdhīrastatra na muhyati
2.13.gloss: As the embodied one passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it passes on to another body; the composed one is not misled by this.

2.20.iast: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin | nāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ . | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṃ purāṇo | na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre
2.20.gloss: It is never born, nor does it ever die; having once been, it never ceases to be — unborn, eternal, everlasting, primeval, it is not killed when the body is killed.
2.20.note: The Gita's most quoted statement of the self. It assumes rebirth as background, not as something to prove.

2.22.iast: vāsāṃsi jīrṇāni yathā vihāya | navāni gṛhṇāti naro'parāṇi . | tathā śarīrāṇi vihāya jīrṇā- | nyanyāni saṃyāti navāni dehī
2.22.gloss: As a man casts off worn-out garments and puts on new ones, so the embodied one casts off worn-out bodies and takes up others that are new.

2.23.iast: nainaṃ chindanti śastrāṇi nainaṃ dahati pāvakaḥ . | na cainaṃ kledayantyāpo na śoṣayati mārutaḥ
2.23.gloss: Weapons do not cut it; fire does not burn it; waters do not wet it; wind does not wither it.

2.27.iast: jātasya hi dhruvo mṛtyurdhruvaṃ janma mṛtasya ca . | tasmādaparihārye'rthe na tvaṃ śocitumarhasi
2.27.gloss: For one who is born, death is certain; for one who is dead, birth is certain; over this, which cannot be otherwise, you should not grieve.

2.31.iast: svadharmamapi cāvekṣya na vikampitumarhasi . | dharmyāddhi yuddhācchreyo'nyatkṣatriyasya na vidyate
2.31.gloss: And as regards your own duty, you should not waver: for a kshatriya there is nothing better than a battle lawful by dharma.
2.31.note: The chapter pivots here from the metaphysics of the self to the argument from warrior duty — svadharma.

2.32.iast: yadṛcchayā copapannaṃ svargadvāramapāvṛtam . | sukhinaḥ kṣatriyāḥ pārtha labhante yuddhamīdṛśam
2.32.gloss: Kshatriyas who meet with such a battle, Partha, a chance-opened gate of heaven, are the fortunate ones.

2.37.iast: hato vā prāpsyasi svargaṃ jitvā vā bhokṣyase mahīm . | tasmāduttiṣṭha kaunteya yuddhāya kṛtaniścayaḥ
2.37.gloss: Slain — you will win heaven; victorious — you will enjoy the earth. Rise therefore, son of Kunti, your mind made up to fight.

2.38.iast: sukhaduḥkhe same kṛtvā lābhālābhau jayājayau . | tato yuddhāya yujyasva naivaṃ pāpamavāpsyasi
2.38.gloss: Making pleasure and pain the same, gain and loss, victory and defeat — gird for battle then; so you will incur no wrong.
2.38.note: 'Pāpam' here ranges from 'sin' to 'wrong' to 'misfortune'; translations differ.

2.39.iast: eṣā te'bhihitā sāṅkhye buddhiryoge tvimāṃ śṛṇu . | buddhyā yukto yayā pārtha karmabandhaṃ prahāsyasi
2.39.gloss: This much has been set out by way of analysis; now hear it in yoga: yoked by this understanding, Partha, you will cast off the bond of action.
2.39.note: 'Sāṅkhya' here means analysis/discipline of knowledge; 'buddhi-yoga' the disciplined intelligence applied to action.

2.47.iast: karmaṇyevādhikāraste mā phaleṣu kadācana . | mā karmaphalaheturbhūrmā te saṅgo'stvakarmaṇi
2.47.gloss: Your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits; do not let the fruits be your motive; neither let there be attachment to inaction.
2.47.note: The most translated verse of the Gita. 'Adhikāra' = right/claim/jurisdiction; 'phala-hetu' = cause/reason-in-the-fruit. Whether this counsels detachment from outcome, selfless service, devotional service, or psychological non-clutching is the fork the whole book turns on.

2.48.iast: yogasthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā dhanañjaya . | siddhyasiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṃ yoga ucyate
2.48.gloss: Established in yoga, do your work, letting go of attachment, Dhanañjaya; even in success and failure — that evenness is called yoga.

2.54.iast: sthitaprajñasya kā bhāṣā samādhisthasya keśava . | sthitadhīḥ kiṃ prabhāṣeta kimāsīta vrajeta kim
2.54.gloss: Arjuna: What is the description of the one of steady wisdom, of the one stable in absorption? How does the settled one speak, sit, walk about?

2.55.iast: prajahāti yadā kāmānsarvānpārtha manogatān . | ātmanyevātmanā tuṣṭaḥ sthitaprajñastadocyate
2.55.gloss: Krishna: When he casts off all the desires of the mind, content in the self alone through the self, he is said to be of steady wisdom.

2.62.iast: dhyāyato viṣayānpuṃsaḥ saṅgasteṣūpajāyate . | saṅgātsañjāyate kāmaḥ kāmātkrodho'bhijāyate
2.62.gloss: In one who broods on sense-objects, attachment to them is born; from attachment, desire is born; from desire, anger is born.
2.62.note: The Gita's causal chain of moral failure: attention → attachment → desire → anger. It is quoted in management and psychology writing as much as in theology.

2.63.iast: krodhādbhavati sammohaḥ sammohātsmṛtivibhramaḥ . | smṛtibhraṃśād buddhināśo buddhināśātpraṇaśyati
2.63.gloss: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, loss of memory; from lost memory, the ruin of discernment; with discernment ruined, he is destroyed.

2.70.iast: āpūryamāṇamacalapratiṣṭhaṃ | samudramāpaḥ praviśanti yadvat . | tadvatkāmā yaṃ praviśanti sarve | sa śāntimāpnoti na kāmakāmī
2.70.gloss: As the waters enter a full, unmoving sea from every side, so into such a one all desires enter — he attains peace, not the desire-chaser.

2.72.iast: eṣā brāhmī sthitiḥ pārtha naināṃ prāpya vimuhyati . | sthitvāsyāmantakāle'pi brahmanirvāṇamṛcchati
2.72.gloss: This is the state established in brahman, Partha; having reached it, one is not deluded; established in it even at the hour of death, one attains nirvana in brahman.
2.72.note: The Gita uses the Buddhist term 'nirvāṇa' here — one thread in the debate about its relation to Buddhist thought.

3.5.iast: na hi kaścitkṣaṇamapi jātu tiṣṭhatyakarmakṛt . | kāryate hyavaśaḥ karma sarvaḥ prakṛtijairguṇaiḥ
3.5.gloss: No one rests even for a moment without acting; all beings are made to act by the strands born of nature.

3.9.iast: yajñārthātkarmaṇo'nyatra loko'yaṃ karmabandhanaḥ . | tadarthaṃ karma kaunteya muktasaṅgaḥ samācara
3.9.gloss: Action other than for sacrifice binds this world; acting for that end, be free of attachment, son of Kunti.
3.9.note: 'Yajña' (sacrifice/offering) is reinterpreted through the Gita from ritual offering to dedicated, other-regarding action.

3.19.iast: tasmādasaktaḥ satataṃ kāryaṃ karma samācara . | asakto hyācarankarma paramāpnoti pūruṣaḥ
3.19.gloss: Therefore, unattached, always do what work is to be done; the unattached one doing work attains the highest.

3.27.iast: prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni guṇaiḥ karmāṇi sarvaśaḥ . | ahaṅkāravimūḍhātmā kartāhamiti manyate
3.27.gloss: All actions are performed by the strands of nature in every way; one deluded by ego thinks, 'I am the doer.'

3.35.iast: śreyānsvadharmo viguṇaḥ paradharmātsvanuṣṭhitāt . | svadharme nidhanaṃ śreyaḥ paradharmo bhayāvahaḥ
3.35.gloss: Better is one's own duty though flawed, than another's duty well done; better is death in one's own duty — another's duty is full of fear.
3.35.note: With 18.47, the most socially consequential verse of the Gita: read as vocational integrity by some, as birth-duty apologetics by others.

3.37.iast: kāma eṣa krodha eṣa rajoguṇasamudbhavaḥ . | mahāśano mahāpāpmā viddhyenamiha vairiṇam
3.37.gloss: It is desire, it is anger, born of the strand of passion, all-devouring, most impure — know this here as the enemy.

3.42.iast: indriyāṇi parāṇyāhurindriyebhyaḥ paraṃ manaḥ . | manasastu parā buddhiryo buddheḥ paratastu saḥ
3.42.gloss: The senses, they say, are higher than the body; higher than the senses, the mind; higher than the mind, discernment; and higher than discernment, that.
3.42.note: The last 'that' (saḥ) is read as the self or as the lord, depending on the commentator.

3.43.iast: evaṃ buddheḥ paraṃ buddhvā saṃstabhyātmānamātmanā . | jahi śatruṃ mahābāho kāmarūpaṃ durāsadam
3.43.gloss: Thus knowing it as higher than discernment, steadying the self by the self, strike down this enemy in the form of desire, so hard to master, mighty-armed one.

4.1.iast: imaṃ vivasvate yogaṃ proktavānahamavyayam . | vivasvānmanave prāha manurikṣvākave'bravīt
4.1.gloss: I spoke this imperishable yoga to Vivasvan the sun; Vivasvan spoke it to Manu; Manu spoke it to Ikshvaku.
4.1.note: The genealogy frames the Gita as an eternal teaching restored — the verse Bhaktivedanta Swami builds his 'disciplic succession' reading on.

4.2.iast: evaṃ paramparāprāptamimaṃ rājarṣayo viduḥ . | sa kāleneha mahatā yogo naṣṭaḥ parantapa
4.2.gloss: Thus received down the line, the royal seers knew it; by the great lapse of time this yoga was lost here, burner of foes.

4.6.iast: ajo'pi sannavyayātmā bhūtānāmīśvaro'pi san . | prakṛtiṃ svāmadhiṣṭhāya sambhavāmyātmamāyayā
4.6.gloss: Though unborn, of imperishable self, and lord of beings — resting on my own nature I come to be by my own māyā.
4.6.note: 'Māyā' here means the lord's own power of self-manifestation, not (yet) 'illusion'. Shankara and the Vaishnava schools part ways over this word.

4.7.iast: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānirbhavati bhārata . | abhyutthānamadharmasya tadātmānaṃ sṛjāmyaham
4.7.gloss: Whenever dharma declines, Bharata, and adharma rises — I bring myself into being.
4.7.note: The avatāra doctrine in two lines. The word 'avatāra' itself never appears in the Gita; the concept does.

4.8.iast: paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṃ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām . | dharmasaṃsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge
4.8.gloss: To shelter the good, to destroy the wicked, to set dharma on its feet — I come into being age after age.

4.13.iast: cāturvarṇyaṃ mayā sṛṣṭaṃ guṇakarmavibhāgaśaḥ . | tasya kartāramapi māṃ viddhyakartāramavyayam
4.13.gloss: The four-varna order I made, according to strand and action; though its maker, know me as non-maker, imperishable.
4.13.note: The fork of forks. 'Guṇa-karma' = 'by quality and function' or 'by quality-born action' — read as anti-birth by some devotee commentators, as divine sanction of hierarchy by critics such as Ambedkar, and as a later interpolation by some historians.

4.34.iast: tadviddhi praṇipātena paripraśnena sevayā . | upadekṣyanti te jñānaṃ jñāninastattvadarśinaḥ
4.34.gloss: Know this by bowing, by asking, by serving; those who see the real will teach you knowledge.
4.34.note: The Gita's teacher-verse: prostration, inquiry, service — claimed by every guru-led tradition.

4.37.iast: yathaidhāṃsi samiddho'gnirbhasmasātkurute'rjuna . | jñānāgniḥ sarvakarmāṇi bhasmasātkurute tathā
4.37.gloss: As a fire well-lit turns kindling to ash, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge turns all actions to ash.

4.38.iast: na hi jñānena sadṛśaṃ pavitramiha vidyate . | tatsvayaṃ yogasaṃsiddhaḥ kālenātmani vindati
4.38.gloss: Nothing that purifies equals knowledge; perfected in yoga, one finds it in oneself in time.

5.2.iast: saṃnyāsaḥ karmayogaśca niḥśreyasakarāvubhau . | tayostu karmasaṃnyāsātkarmayogo viśiṣyate
5.2.gloss: Both renunciation and karma-yoga carry one to the highest; of the two, karma-yoga excels renunciation of action.
5.2.note: The verdict Tilak built his whole Gita Rahasya on.

5.8.gloss: The one yoked in knowledge, knowing the real, thinks 'I do nothing at all' — while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing.

5.9.gloss: Speaking, releasing, taking, opening and closing the eyes, he holds firmly: 'it is the senses that move among their objects.'

5.18.iast: vidyāvinayasampanne brāhmaṇe gavi hastini . | śuni caiva śvapāke ca paṇḍitāḥ samadarśinaḥ
5.18.gloss: The learned see the same in a brahmin of learning and courtesy, in a cow, in an elephant, in a dog — and in a dog-cooker.
5.18.note: 'Śvapāka' literally 'dog-cooker', an outcaste occupation. The verse's radical equality claim coexists in the same text with 4.13 and 18.41 — a tension every reader must place somewhere.

5.29.iast: bhoktāraṃ yajñatapasāṃ sarvalokamaheśvaram . | suhṛdaṃ sarvabhūtānāṃ jñātvā māṃ śāntimṛcchati
5.29.gloss: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, as the great lord of all worlds, as the friend of all beings — one attains peace.

6.5.iast: uddharedātmanātmānaṃ nātmānamavasādayet . | ātmaiva hyātmano bandhurātmaiva ripurātmanaḥ
6.5.gloss: Let a man lift himself by himself; let him not degrade himself; the self alone is the self's friend, the self alone its enemy.
6.5.note: One of the Gita's most-quoted self-reliance verses — 'uddhared ātmanātmānam'.

6.16.iast: nātyaśnatastu yogo'sti na caikāntamanaśnataḥ . | na cātisvapnaśīlasya jāgrato naiva cārjuna
6.16.gloss: Yoga is not for one who overeats, Arjuna, nor for one who does not eat at all; nor for one who oversleeps, nor for one who keeps awake.

6.17.iast: yuktāhāravihārasya yuktaceṣṭasya karmasu . | yuktasvapnāvabodhasya yogo bhavati duḥkhahā
6.17.gloss: For one measured in eating and in recreation, measured in effort, measured in sleeping and waking — yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.
6.17.note: The 'moderation verse' — often quoted as the Gita's middle way, echoing Buddhist phrasing.

6.19.iast: yathā dīpo nivātastho neṅgate sopamā smṛtā . | yogino yatacittasya yuñjato yogamātmanaḥ
6.19.gloss: As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker — so runs the likeness of the yogi of subdued mind, practicing yoga of the self.

6.34.iast: cañcalaṃ hi manaḥ kṛṣṇa pramāthi balavad dṛḍham . | tasyāhaṃ nigrahaṃ manye vāyoriva suduṣkaram
6.34.gloss: Arjuna: The mind is restless, Krishna — turbulent, powerful, obstinate; to curb it seems to me as hard as to curb the wind.

6.35.iast: asaṃśayaṃ mahābāho mano durnigrahaṃ calam . | abhyāsena tu kaunteya vairāgyeṇa ca gṛhyate
6.35.gloss: Krishna: No doubt, mighty-armed one — the mind is restless and hard to curb; yet by practice and by non-attachment, son of Kunti, it is held.

6.47.iast: yogināmapi sarveṣāṃ madgatenāntarātmanā . | śraddhāvānbhajate yo māṃ sa me yuktatamo mataḥ
6.47.gloss: And of all yogis, the one who worships me with faith, his self absorbed in me — that one I hold the most yoked of all.
6.47.note: Chapter 6, devoted to meditation, ends by ranking the devotee above the meditator — a hinge toward the devotion chapters.

7.5.iast: apareyamitastvanyāṃ prakṛtiṃ viddhi me parām . | jīvabhūtāṃ mahābāho yayedaṃ dhāryate jagat
7.5.gloss: This is my lower nature; know my other, higher nature — the life-element, mighty-armed one, by which this world is held fast.
7.5.note: The Gita's two-natures doctrine: matter (apara prakṛti) and life/soul (para prakṛti).

7.14.iast: daivī hyeṣā guṇamayī mama māyā duratyayā . | māmeva ye prapadyante māyāmetāṃ taranti te
7.14.gloss: For divine is this strand-woven māyā of mine, hard to cross; those who take refuge in me alone cross over this māyā.

7.16.iast: caturvidhā bhajante māṃ janāḥ sukṛtino'rjuna . | ārto jijñāsurarthārthī jñānī ca bharatarṣabha
7.16.gloss: Four kinds of virtuous folk worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the knowledge-seeker, the wealth-seeker — and the wise.

7.19.iast: bahūnāṃ janmanāmante jñānavānmāṃ prapadyate . | vāsudevaḥ sarvamiti sa mahātmā sudurlabhaḥ
7.19.gloss: At the end of many births, the wise one comes to refuge in me: 'Vasudeva is everything.' Such a great soul is very rare.

7.21.iast: yo yo yāṃ yāṃ tanuṃ bhaktaḥ śraddhayārcitumicchati . | tasya tasyācalāṃ śraddhāṃ tāmeva vidadhāmyaham
7.21.gloss: Whatever form any devotee wishes to worship in faith — that very faith of theirs I make firm.
7.21.note: The Gita's most pluralism-friendly verse: other gods are given a place within Krishna's economy.

7.22.iast: sa tayā śraddhayā yuktastasyārādhanamīhate . | labhate ca tataḥ kāmānmayaiva vihitānhi tān
7.22.gloss: Yoked in that faith, such a one seeks the favor of that form — and from it gains the desires wished; the arranging is mine.

8.3.iast: akṣaraṃ brahma paramaṃ svabhāvo'dhyātmamucyate . | bhūtabhāvodbhavakaro visargaḥ karmasaṃjñitaḥ
8.3.gloss: The imperishable — that is the highest brahman; its dwelling in each body is called the self; the letting-forth that brings beings to birth is called action.
8.3.note: The Gita defining its own key terms: brahman, adhyātma, karma.

8.5.iast: antakāle ca māmeva smaranmuktvā kalevaram . | yaḥ prayāti sa madbhāvaṃ yāti nāstyatra saṃśayaḥ
8.5.gloss: Whoever, at the time of death, lets go of the body remembering me alone — that one goes to my being; there is no doubt.

8.6.iast: yaṃ yaṃ vāpi smaranbhāvaṃ tyajatyante kalevaram . | taṃ tamevaiti kaunteya sadā tadbhāvabhāvitaḥ
8.6.gloss: Whatever state of being one remembers when quitting the body at the end — to that very state one goes, always made of that memory.

8.7.gloss: Therefore at all times remember me — and fight. With mind and understanding entrusted to me, you shall come to me; there is no doubt.
8.7.note: 'Remember me and fight' — devotion and battle in one breath; the verse that most embarrasses pacifist readings and energizes activist ones.

8.22.iast: puruṣaḥ sa paraḥ pārtha bhaktyā labhyastvananyayā . | yasyāntaḥsthāni bhūtāni yena sarvamidaṃ tatam
8.22.gloss: That is the highest person, Partha, in whom beings dwell, by whom all this is pervaded — attained by devotion and by nothing else.

9.4.iast: mayā tatamidaṃ sarvaṃ jagadavyaktamūrtinā . | matsthāni sarvabhūtāni na cāhaṃ teṣvavasthitaḥ
9.4.gloss: All this world is pervaded by me in unmanifest form; in me all beings stand — yet I do not stand in them.
9.4.note: The classic panentheist formula: God in the world, the world in God, and yet not identical.

9.22.iast: ananyāścintayanto māṃ ye janāḥ paryupāsate . | teṣāṃ nityābhiyuktānāṃ yogakṣemaṃ vahāmyaham
9.22.gloss: Those who, meditating, worship me with minds nowhere else — I myself carry for them, ever-yoked ones, their yoga and their kshema.
9.22.note: 'Yoga-kṣema' is a technical pair: what is attained and what is safeguarded. Rendered variously as 'what they need and what they have'.

9.26.iast: patraṃ puṣpaṃ phalaṃ toyaṃ yo me bhaktyā prayacchati . | tadahaṃ bhaktyupahṛtamaśnāmi prayatātmanaḥ
9.26.gloss: A leaf, a flower, a fruit, water — whoever offers it to me with devotion, that I receive from the striving soul.

9.29.iast: samo'haṃ sarvabhūteṣu na me dveṣyo'sti na priyaḥ . | ye bhajanti tu māṃ bhaktyā mayi te teṣu cāpyaham
9.29.gloss: I am the same toward all beings; to me none is hateful, and none is dear; but those who worship me with devotion are in me — and I in them.

9.30.iast: api cetsudurācāro bhajate māmananyabhāk . | sādhureva sa mantavyaḥ samyagvyavasito hi saḥ
9.30.gloss: Even if one of utterly wicked conduct worships me with single devotion, that one is to be counted righteous — rightly resolved.

9.31.iast: kṣipraṃ bhavati dharmātmā śaśvacchāntiṃ nigacchati . | kaunteya pratijānīhi na me bhaktaḥ praṇaśyati
9.31.gloss: Soon he becomes a man of dharma and attains lasting peace; know this for certain, son of Kunti: my devotee is never lost.

9.32.iast: māṃ hi pārtha vyapāśritya ye'pi syuḥ pāpayonayaḥ . | striyo vaiśyāstathā śūdrāste'pi yānti parāṃ gatim
9.32.gloss: Taking refuge in me, even those born of ill wombs — women, vaishyas, shudras likewise — even they go the highest way.
9.32.note: The Gita's most debated inclusion verse: does 'even they' open heaven's door to the excluded, or confirm who was excluded? Read both ways across two millennia.

9.34.iast: manmanā bhava madbhakto madyājī māṃ namaskuru . | māmevaiṣyasi yuktvaivamātmānaṃ matparāyaṇaḥ
9.34.gloss: Set your mind on me, be my devotee, sacrifice to me, bow to me; yoked to me, with me as your highest end — you will come to me.

10.8.iast: ahaṃ sarvasya prabhavo mattaḥ sarvaṃ pravartate . | iti matvā bhajante māṃ budhā bhāvasamanvitāḥ
10.8.gloss: I am the source of all; from me everything moves onward; knowing this, the wise worship me, moved by feeling.

10.20.iast: ahamātmā guḍākeśa sarvabhūtāśayasthitaḥ . | ahamādiśca madhyaṃ ca bhūtānāmanta eva ca
10.20.gloss: I am the self seated in the hearts of all beings, Gudakesha; I am the beginning and the middle, and the end too of beings.

10.41.iast: yadyadvibhūtimatsattvaṃ śrīmadūrjitameva vā . | tattadevāvagaccha tvaṃ mama tejoṃ'śasambhavam
10.41.gloss: Whatever being has glory, or beauty, or strength — know it as born of a spark of my splendor.
10.41.note: Oppenheimer's 'brighter than a thousand suns' belongs to this chapter's neighborhood (11.12) — radiance as a divine signature.

11.12.iast: divi sūryasahasrasya bhavedyugapadutthitā . | yadi bhāḥ sadṛśī sā syādbhāsastasya mahātmanaḥ
11.12.gloss: If the light of a thousand suns were to rise at once in the sky, that might resemble the splendor of that great one.
11.12.note: The verse behind 'brighter than a thousand suns' — though the exact English phrasing comes from Robert Jungk's 1958 retelling of Oppenheimer, not from Oppenheimer's own lips at Trinity.

11.28.iast: yathā nadīnāṃ bahavo'mbuvegāḥ | samudramevābhimukhā dravanti . | tathā tavāmī naralokavīrā | viśanti vaktrāṇyabhivijvalanti
11.28.gloss: As the many streams of rivers run headlong into the ocean, so these heroes of the world of men enter your blazing mouths.

11.32.iast: kālo'smi lokakṣayakṛtpravṛddho | lokānsamāhartumiha pravṛttaḥ . | ṛte'pi tvāṃ na bhaviṣyanti sarve | ye'vasthitāḥ pratyanīkeṣu yodhāḥ
11.32.gloss: I am time, grown great, the destroyer of worlds, set in motion here to gather in the worlds; even without you, none of these warriors in the opposing ranks shall remain.
11.32.note: 'Kāla' = time, not 'death' (that is mṛtyu). Oppenheimer's 'Now I am become Death' follows his teacher Ryder's rendering. Readings differ on what identifying with 'time' does to the speaker's guilt.

11.33.iast: tasmāttvamuttiṣṭha yaśo labhasva | jitvā śatrūn bhuṅkṣva rājyaṃ samṛddham . | mayaivaite nihatāḥ pūrvameva | nimittamātraṃ bhava savyasācin
11.33.gloss: Therefore rise, win glory; conquering your enemies, enjoy a flourishing kingdom. By me these have already been slain — be you merely the instrument, left-handed archer.
11.33.note: 'Nimitta-mātra' = mere instrument/occasion. The strongest verse for the 'divine determinism' reading — and the one Ambedkar called a lunatic's defense of murder.

11.53.iast: nāhaṃ vedairna tapasā na dānena na cejyayā . | śakya evaṃvidho draṣṭuṃ dṛṣṭavānasi māṃ yathā
11.53.gloss: Not by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by giving, nor by ritual — can I be seen as you have seen me.

11.54.iast: bhaktyā tvananyayā śakya ahamevaṃvidho'rjuna . | jñātuṃ draṣṭuṃ ca tattvena praveṣṭuṃ ca parantapa
11.54.gloss: By unwavering devotion alone can I be known in this way, Arjuna — seen in truth, entered into.

11.55.iast: matkarmakṛnmatparamo madbhaktaḥ saṅgavarjitaḥ . | nirvairaḥ sarvabhūteṣu yaḥ sa māmeti pāṇḍava
11.55.gloss: Who works for me, holds me supreme, is devoted to me, free of attachment, bearing no enmity toward any being — that one comes to me, Pandava.

12.2.iast: mayyāveśya mano ye māṃ nityayuktā upāsate . | śraddhayā parayopetāḥ te me yuktatamā matāḥ
12.2.gloss: Those who set their minds on me, ever-yoked, worshipping with supreme faith — them I hold the highest.

12.5.gloss: For those attached to the unmanifest, the struggle is greater; the way of the unmanifest is hard for the embodied to attain.

12.13.iast: adveṣṭā sarvabhūtānāṃ maitraḥ karuṇa eva ca . | nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ samaduḥkhasukhaḥ kṣamī
12.13.gloss: Free of ill-will toward all beings, friendly, compassionate; without possessiveness, without ego; even in pain and pleasure, patient.

12.14.iast: santuṣṭaḥ satataṃ yogī yatātmā dṛḍhaniścayaḥ . | mayyarpitamanobuddhiryo madbhaktaḥ sa me priyaḥ
12.14.gloss: Content, ever a yogi, self-possessed, firm of resolve; with mind and understanding offered to me — my devotee, dear to me.

12.15.iast: yasmānnodvijate loko lokānnodvijate ca yaḥ . | harṣāmarṣabhayodvegairmukto yaḥ sa ca me priyaḥ
12.15.gloss: He from whom the world is not disturbed, and who is not disturbed by the world; freed from delight, envy, fear and dread — dear to me.

12.16.iast: anapekṣaḥ śucirdakṣa udāsīno gatavyathaḥ . | sarvārambhaparityāgī yo madbhaktaḥ sa me priyaḥ
12.16.gloss: Asking nothing, pure, capable, indifferent, untroubled, letting go of every undertaking — my devotee, dear to me.

13.1.iast: prakṛtiṃ puruṣaṃ caiva kṣetraṃ kṣetrajñameva ca . | etadveditumicchāmi jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ ca keśava
13.1.gloss: Arjuna: Nature and the person, the field and the knower of the field, knowledge and the knowable — these I wish to know, Keshava.

13.2.iast: idaṃ śarīraṃ kaunteya kṣetramityabhidhīyate . | etadyo vetti taṃ prāhuḥ kṣetrajña iti tadvidaḥ
13.2.gloss: Krishna: This body is called the field, son of Kunti; and the one who knows it — those who know call that one the knower of the field.

13.7.iast: icchā dveṣaḥ sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ saṅghātaścetanā dhṛtiḥ . | etatkṣetraṃ samāsena savikāramudāhṛtam
13.7.gloss: Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, awareness, resolve — this, in brief, with its workings, is what is called the field.

13.8.gloss: Humility, unpretentiousness, non-injury, patience, uprightness; serving the teacher, purity, steadiness, self-restraint.

13.19.iast: iti kṣetraṃ tathā jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ coktaṃ samāsataḥ . | madbhakta etadvijñāya madbhāvāyopapadyate
13.19.gloss: Thus have the field, knowledge and the knowable been set out in brief; my devotee, knowing this, enters into my being.

13.20.iast: prakṛtiṃ puruṣaṃ caiva viddhyanādī ubhāvapi . | vikārāṃśca guṇāṃścaiva viddhi prakṛtisambhavān
13.20.gloss: Know nature and the person alike as without beginning; know the alterations and the strands as born of nature.

13.23.iast: upadraṣṭānumantā ca bhartā bhoktā maheśvaraḥ . | paramātmeti cāpyukto dehe'sminpuruṣaḥ paraḥ
13.23.gloss: The witness, the permitter, the supporter, the enjoyer, the great lord — and what is also called the highest self — this is the person in this body.

13.27.gloss: Whatever comes into being, moving or unmoving — know, bull of Bharata, that it is born of the union of the field and its knower.

13.28.iast: samaṃ sarveṣu bhūteṣu tiṣṭhantaṃ parameśvaram . | vinaśyatsvavinaśyantaṃ yaḥ paśyati sa paśyati
13.28.gloss: Who sees the same lord standing within all beings, perishing as they perish — that one truly sees.

14.5.iast: sattvaṃ rajastama iti guṇāḥ prakṛtisambhavāḥ . | nibadhnanti mahābāho dehe dehinamavyayam
14.5.gloss: Strand-lucidity, passion and inertia — these strands, born of nature, bind the embodied one, the imperishable, fast in the body.

14.6.iast: tatra sattvaṃ nirmalatvātprakāśakamanāmayam . | sukhasaṅgena badhnāti jñānasaṅgena cānagha
14.6.gloss: Of these, lucidity — stainless, luminous, unailing — binds through attachment to happiness and to knowledge.

14.7.iast: rajo rāgātmakaṃ viddhi tṛṣṇāsaṅgasamudbhavam . | tannibadhnāti kaunteya karmasaṅgena dehinam
14.7.gloss: Know passion as born of desire, attachment-bred; it binds the embodied one, son of Kunti, by attachment to action.

14.8.iast: tamastvajñānajaṃ viddhi mohanaṃ sarvadehinām . | pramādālasyanidrābhistannibadhnāti bhārata
14.8.gloss: And know inertia as born of ignorance, bewildering all embodied beings; it binds through heedlessness, sloth and sleep.

14.19.iast: nānyaṃ guṇebhyaḥ kartāraṃ yadā draṣṭānupaśyati . | guṇebhyaśca paraṃ vetti madbhāvaṃ so'dhigacchati
14.19.gloss: When the seer sees no doer apart from the strands, and knows what is beyond the strands — that one reaches my being.
14.19.note: The mechanistic fork: if the strands do everything, where is free will? Chapter 14's determinism is the text's sharpest.

14.26.iast: māṃ ca yo'vyabhicāreṇa bhaktiyogena sevate . | sa guṇānsamatītyaitānbrahmabhūyāya kalpate
14.26.gloss: And whoever serves me with unwavering devotion — that one crosses beyond these strands and is made fit for brahman.

15.1.iast: ūrdhvamūlamadhaḥśākhamaśvatthaṃ prāhuravyayam . | chandāṃsi yasya parṇāni yastaṃ veda sa vedavit
15.1.gloss: They speak of an imperishable banyan, roots above, branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns; who knows it, knows the Vedas.
15.1.note: 'Aśvattha' = the banyan/peepul fig — 'that which will not stand the same till tomorrow', an etymology the tradition savors.

15.2.iast: adhaścordhvaṃ prasṛtāstasya śākhā | guṇapravṛddhā viṣayapravālāḥ . | adhaśca mūlānyanusantatāni | karmānubandhīni manuṣyaloke
15.2.gloss: Below and above stretch its branches, grown by the strands, their shoots the sense-fields; and its secondary roots run below, binding through action, in the world of humans.

15.3.iast: na rūpamasyeha tathopalabhyate | nānto na cādirna ca sampratiṣṭhā . | aśvatthamenaṃ suvirūḍhamūlaṃ | asaṅgaśastreṇa dṛḍhena chittvā
15.3.gloss: Its form here is not grasped like that — no end, no beginning, no resting place. This banyan of firm-rooted form is to be cut down with the strong axe of non-attachment.

15.4.iast: tataḥ padaṃ tatparimārgitavyaṃ | yasmingatā na nivartanti bhūyaḥ . | tameva cādyaṃ puruṣaṃ prapadye . | yataḥ pravṛttiḥ prasṛtā purāṇī
15.4.gloss: Then that resting-place is to be sought, going where one does not return again: 'I take refuge in that first person from whom this ancient current set forth.'

15.6.iast: na tadbhāsayate sūryo na śaśāṅko na pāvakaḥ . | yadgatvā na nivartante taddhāma paramaṃ mama
15.6.gloss: That, my highest abode, is lit by neither sun nor moon nor fire; going there, none return.

15.15.iast: sarvasya cāhaṃ hṛdi sanniviṣṭo | mattaḥ smṛtirjñānamapohanañca . | vedaiśca sarvairahameva vedyo | vedāntakṛdvedavideva cāham
15.15.gloss: And I am seated in the hearts of all; from me come memory, knowledge and their loss; by all the Vedas I alone am to be known; I am the maker of Vedanta, the knower of the Veda.

15.16.iast: dvāvimau puruṣau loke kṣaraścākṣara eva ca . | kṣaraḥ sarvāṇi bhūtāni kūṭastho'kṣara ucyate
15.16.gloss: There are two persons in this world: the perishable and the imperishable; the perishable is all beings; the fixed one is called the imperishable.

15.17.iast: uttamaḥ puruṣastvanyaḥ paramātmetyudāhṛtaḥ . | yo lokatrayamāviśya bibhartyavyaya īśvaraḥ
15.17.gloss: But other than both is the highest person, called the highest self — entering the three worlds, upholding them, the imperishable lord.

15.18.iast: yasmātkṣaramatīto'hamakṣarādapi cottamaḥ . | ato'smi loke vede ca prathitaḥ puruṣottamaḥ
15.18.gloss: Because I am beyond the perishable, and higher even than the imperishable — in the world and in the Veda I am celebrated as the highest person.
15.18.note: The 'puruṣottama' three-tier ontology — the verse that gives the chapter its name.

16.1.iast: abhayaṃ sattvasaṃśuddhirjñānayogavyavasthitiḥ . | dānaṃ damaśca yajñaśca svādhyāyastapa ārjavam
16.1.gloss: Fearlessness, purity of one's being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge; giving, self-restraint, sacrifice, recitation, austerity, uprightness.

16.2.iast: ahiṃsā satyamakrodhastyāgaḥ śāntirapaiśunam . | dayā bhūteṣvaloluptvaṃ mārdavaṃ hrīracāpalam
16.2.gloss: Non-injury, truth, absence of anger, relinquishing, calm, non-slander; compassion for beings, freedom from craving, gentleness, modesty, steadiness.

16.3.iast: tejaḥ kṣamā dhṛtiḥ śaucamadroho nātimānitā . | bhavanti sampadaṃ daivīmabhijātasya bhārata
16.3.gloss: Vigor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, freedom from envy, absence of pride — these are of one born to the divine estate.

16.4.iast: dambho darpo'bhimānaśca krodhaḥ pāruṣyameva ca . | ajñānaṃ cābhijātasya pārtha sampadamāsurīm
16.4.gloss: Ostentation, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, harshness, ignorance — these are of one born to the demonic estate.

16.8.gloss: They say the world is unreal, without foundation, without a lord; born of mutual union — of desire alone, without other cause.
16.8.note: The Gita's sketch of nihilists — often read as a swipe at materialist (Cārvāka) and some Buddhist schools.

16.13.iast: idamadya mayā labdhamimaṃ prāpsye manoratham . | idamastīdamapi me bhaviṣyati punardhanam
16.13.gloss: 'This I have gained today; this desire I shall fulfill; this much is mine — and this wealth too shall be mine.'
16.13.note: The Gita ventriloquizes the demonic self — the only place it stages an inner monologue.

16.14.iast: asau mayā hataḥ śatrurhaniṣye cāparānapi . | īśvaro'hamahaṃ bhogī siddho'haṃ balavānsukhī
16.14.gloss: 'That enemy has been slain by me; these others too I shall slay. I am lord, I am enjoyer, I am perfected, mighty, happy.'

16.21.iast: trividhaṃ narakasyedaṃ dvāraṃ nāśanamātmanaḥ . | kāmaḥ krodhastathā lobhastasmādetattrayaṃ tyajet
16.21.gloss: Threefold is the gate of hell, ruinous to the self: desire, anger and greed; therefore let a man abandon these three.

16.23.iast: yaḥ śāstravidhimutsṛjya vartate kāmakārataḥ . | na sa siddhimavāpnoti na sukhaṃ na parāṃ gatim
16.23.gloss: Who, casting off the rule of scripture, acts by whim of desire — attains no perfection, no happiness, no highest way.

16.24.iast: tasmācchāstraṃ pramāṇaṃ te kāryākāryavyavasthitau . | jñātvā śāstravidhānoktaṃ karma kartumihārhasi
16.24.gloss: Therefore, let scripture be your measure for what is to be done and not done; knowing the rule of scripture, act here.
16.24.note: The Gita's own statement of textual authority — the verse that makes the commentator's job sacred, and the reformer's job hard.

17.3.iast: sattvānurūpā sarvasya śraddhā bhavati bhārata . | śraddhāmayo'yaṃ puruṣo yo yacchraddhaḥ sa eva saḥ
17.3.gloss: The faith of each follows its strand; this person is made of faith: whatever one's faith, that is what one is.

17.8.iast: āyuḥsattvabalārogyasukhaprītivivardhanāḥ . | rasyāḥ snigdhāḥ sthirā hṛdyā āhārāḥ sāttvikapriyāḥ
17.8.gloss: Foods that grow life, lucidity, strength, health, gladness, cheer — juicy, unctuous, substantial, agreeable — are dear to the lucid.
17.8.note: The verse behind generations of vegetarian sattvic-diet claims.

17.9.gloss: Foods too bitter, sour, salty, hot, pungent, dry, burning — dear to the passionate — breed pain, grief, sickness.

17.10.iast: yātayāmaṃ gatarasaṃ pūti paryuṣitaṃ ca yat . | ucchiṣṭamapi cāmedhyaṃ bhojanaṃ tāmasapriyam
17.10.gloss: Food stale, tasteless, putrid, left overnight, leavings, unfit for offering — is dear to the inert.

17.15.iast: anudvegakaraṃ vākyaṃ satyaṃ priyahitaṃ ca yat . | svādhyāyābhyasanaṃ caiva vāṅmayaṃ tapa ucyate
17.15.gloss: Speech that gives no offense, that is true, pleasing and beneficial — and the practice of reciting scripture — this is called the austerity of speech.

17.23.iast: oṃtatsaditi nirdeśo brahmaṇastrividhaḥ smṛtaḥ . | brāhmaṇāstena vedāśca yajñāśca vihitāḥ purā
17.23.gloss: 'Oṃ Tat Sat' — this is held to be the threefold designation of brahman; by this were of old marked the brahmins, the Vedas and the sacrifices.

18.1.iast: saṃnyāsasya mahābāho tattvamicchāmi veditum . | tyāgasya ca hṛṣīkeśa pṛthakkeśiniṣūdana
18.1.gloss: Arjuna: I wish to know the truth of renunciation, Hrishikesha, and of letting-go — and their difference, slayer of foes.

18.2.iast: kāmyānāṃ karmaṇāṃ nyāsaṃ saṃnyāsaṃ kavayo viduḥ . | sarvakarmaphalatyāgaṃ prāhustyāgaṃ vicakṣaṇāḥ
18.2.gloss: Krishna: The giving up of desire-driven actions — that the sages call renunciation; the relinquishing of the fruits of all actions — that the discerning call letting-go.
18.2.note: The Gita's closing vocabulary fix: saṃnyāsa vs tyāga. Tilak and Gandhi both hang their readings on this distinction.

18.13.iast: pañcaitāni mahābāho kāraṇāni nibodha me . | sāṅkhye kṛtānte proktāni siddhaye sarvakarmaṇām
18.13.gloss: Learn from me, mighty-armed one, these five causes, as declared in the analysis of the completion of all actions.

18.14.iast: adhiṣṭhānaṃ tathā kartā karaṇaṃ ca pṛthagvidham . | vividhāśca pṛthakceṣṭā daivaṃ caivātra pañcamam
18.14.gloss: The seat or body; the doer; the instruments, various; the several kinds of movement — and the divine, the fifth.

18.15.iast: śarīravāṅmanobhiryatkarma prārabhate naraḥ . | nyāyyaṃ vā viparītaṃ vā pañcaite tasya hetavaḥ
18.15.gloss: Whatever act a person sets going by body, speech or mind — right or wrong — these five are its causes.

18.41.iast: brāhmaṇakṣatriyaviśāṃ śūdrāṇāṃ ca parantapa . | karmāṇi pravibhaktāni svabhāvaprabhavairguṇaiḥ
18.41.gloss: The actions of brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras, scorcher of foes, are distributed by the strands born of each one's own nature.

18.47.iast: śreyānsvadharmo viguṇaḥ paradharmātsvanuṣṭhitāt . | svabhāvaniyataṃ karma kurvannāpnoti kilbiṣam
18.47.gloss: Better one's own duty, though imperfect, than another's well done; acting by the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.
18.47.note: The second svadharma verse. In Sanskrit law-commentary tradition these verses underwrote hereditary occupation; in modern readings they are defended, allegorized or condemned.

18.61.iast: īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ hṛddeśe'rjuna tiṣṭhati . | bhrāmayansarvabhūtāni yantrārūḍhāni māyayā
18.61.gloss: The lord dwells in the hearts of all beings, Arjuna, whirling all beings, seated as if on a machine, by his māyā.
18.61.note: The machine image (yantra) — determinism's sharpest image in the Gita; the verses after it pivot immediately to refuge as the exit.

18.65.iast: manmanā bhava madbhakto madyājī māṃ namaskuru . | māmevaiṣyasi satyaṃ te pratijāne priyo'si me
18.65.gloss: Set your mind on me, be my devotee, sacrifice to me, bow to me; so you will come to me — truly I promise: you are dear to me.

18.66.iast: sarvadharmānparityajya māmekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja . | ahaṃ tvā sarvapāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ
18.66.gloss: Letting go all duties, come take refuge in me alone; I will free you from all wrongs — do not grieve.
18.66.note: The 'charama śloka'. Whether 'abandoning all dharmas' means abandoning works for grace (Ramanuja), or the ego's claim on outcomes (Gandhi), or exclusive devotion (Bhaktivedanta) — this single verse holds the entire interpretive war.

18.73.iast: naṣṭo mohaḥ smṛtirlabdhā tvatprasādānmayācyuta . | sthito'smi gatasandehaḥ kariṣye vacanaṃ tava
18.73.gloss: Arjuna: My delusion is destroyed; memory is recovered — by your grace, unfailing one. I stand, my doubt gone: I will do as you say.
18.73.note: The poem ends with consent, not conviction — Arjuna says 'I will act on your word', and the war proceeds.

18.78.iast: yatra yogeśvaraḥ kṛṣṇo yatra pārtho dhanurdharaḥ . | tatra śrīrvijayo bhūtirdhruvā nītirmatirmama
18.78.gloss: Sanjaya: Where Krishna is the lord of yoga, where Partha is the wielder of the bow — there are splendor, victory, growth, and unshakable counsel — such is my thought.
18.78.note: The closing verse, from the reporter Sanjaya — the Gita's own last word is about the pair: teacher and archer, in that order.
